Regarding the Preface to the *Mahābuddhōṣṇīṣa Sūtra*:
To examine this scripture in detail, it has traditionally lacked a preface. Former sages took the preface to the *Huìjiě* (Comprehensive Explanation) and relocated it to the beginning of the sutra.
This is because its literary style and meaning are complete and its scriptural intent is brilliantly clear.

Indeed, to take the preface to the commentary as the preface to the sūtra itself may be said to exhaustively achieve both beauty and excellence. However, as the time of the preface and the sūtra are vastly different, those who have provided commentaries upon it have been few.
This summer, I accepted an invitation from Longhua in Shanghai with the intention of expounding this sutra. The assembly of practitioners numbered no fewer than two thousand;
however, most were of superficial learning and did not even master the meanings of characters or the divisions of phrases, let alone seek the underlying principles.

At that time, a fellow student requested that I provide a preface for this work, breaking it into sentences and chapters and offering a brief explanation of the terminology, so as to facilitate the understanding of beginners.
I, Ji, received the assistance of those who urged me to ascend the steps toward the heights; unable to decline, I modeled my work after the intent of the *Dharma-paryāya’s* "Propagation" chapter.
I compiled the topical divisions (*ke*), arranged the headings (*mu*), and committed them to writing with detailed explanations, tracing the origins and reaching to the conclusion.

In no more than a few days, the volume was completed, and I entitled it the *Zhimi Shu* (Commentary on Pointing to the Flavor). My intention was that reading the entire sutra is like eating a meal from a large cauldron, whereas studying this commentary is like tasting a single spoonful.
This is merely the flavor of my finger’s touch. The assembly all joined their palms and praised it as excellent. I said: "Although this draft is complete, it is most hasty.
Knowing myself to be like one singing the 'Ba-ge' of the common folk, I dare not present it to the masters of Ying. I only hope that you gentlemen will not weary yourselves by its prolixity."
One must certainly investigate and seek it out before one can attain it; this has never failed to be but a single drop within the ocean of offerings. Someone might say:
"For those who are beginners in the study of the teachings, once they have exhausted the commentaries and sub-commentaries, they remain ignorant of their profound depths;

what benefit, then, do these commentaries provide? I replied: "What words are these? Have you not heard that for those who study wisdom, the goal is to realize what was seen in former lives, and for those who inquire extensively, the value lies in [the accumulation of knowledge]?"

Foreword. This draft is precisely intended for those at the beginning of their practice who wish to easily grasp the essential framework of the entire scripture, so that its key points may be clarified once and for all, preventing the lament of "asking about the bridge.
Could one worry that this is premature planning?

I only hope that superior practitioners engaged in hidden cultivation and noble companions of like mind will first thoroughly read the scriptural text, and only thereafter settle the mind to contemplate the Dharma. Please examine it.

This commentary is broad and comprehensive; by forgetting words and symbols, one attains profound resonance with the ultimate. I pray that the eternal light may manifest at once, causing the sense bases, objects, and consciousnesses to vanish.
If even the Buddha-dharma body and mind are but residual matters, how much more so this deluded consciousness that relies on supernatural powers—is it not indeed superfluous talk? At that time...
Written on the fifth day of the fifth month of the summer in the Gui-si year of the Guangxu era, by the monk Zhuo-san (Di-xian), a late student of the Tiantai school,
who has set down his pen after composing this "Commentary on the Essential Meaning of the Preface to the Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra."
Preface by Chan Master Rulin Tianru of Ancient Wu, Weizé.
Commentary composed by the Bhikṣu Dixian, a descendant of the Tiantai school of Huangyan.

In explaining this preface, the general outline is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the text. The first part is further divided into two sections.
First, the combined explanation; second, the separate explanation. Now, for the first:
the preface to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa*.
This preface establishes its title based on a single dharma. Within this single word "dharma," ten pairs of meanings are contained: namely, teaching and meaning, and nature... [and so forth].

[The six pairs are: practice; phenomenon and principle; object and wisdom; cessation and contemplation; primary and auxiliary; stages and positions; cause and effect; essence and function; and the six levels of identity. First, regarding the pair of teaching and meaning:
"teaching" (jiao) refers to that which expresses, namely the two characters [of the title] in the scripture; "meaning" (yi) refers to that which is expressed.
These refer to the six characters beginning with "Great" (Mahā). This one [character] represents the general meaning, while the nine pairs represent the specific meanings.
Regarding the pair of "nature" (prakṛti) and "cultivation" (bhāvanā) within the explained meanings: "nature" refers to the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa, and "cultivation" refers to the Śūraṅgama.

The intention is to cause people to awaken to the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Dharma, which is the very nature of the mind (*citta-svabhāva*); thus, one first comes to know that cultivation arises from this nature.

Third, regarding the pair of phenomena (*vastu*) and principle (*li*) within the context of cultivation: the Sanskrit term *śūraṅgama* translates into Chinese as "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena.
Here, "phenomena" refers to all phenomena, namely the aggregates (*skandha*), sense bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*).

Furthermore, "principle" (*li*) refers to ultimate solidity; it is the essence of wondrous awakening and clarity. Since one knows that cultivation arises from nature, one must know that cultivation is entirely contained within nature.
Fourth, regarding the unity of object and wisdom (*jñāna*) within the context of phenomena and principle:

the aforementioned phenomena and principle can both serve as objects. One relies on these objects to cultivate contemplation; this contemplation is called wisdom. By means of the object, [wisdom] is elicited.

Because wisdom illuminates the object through wisdom, the fifth point—discussing the pair of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight) within the context of the object and wisdom—is as follows:
the object is that which is contemplated (*ālambana*), and wisdom is that which contemplates (*ālambaka*). The object of contemplation consists of the three truths within a single realm;

the contemplating wisdom consists of the three contemplations within a single mind, which is also the three forms of cessation within a single mind. This is called "Perfect Sudden *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*," because cessation and insight are non-dual.

Therefore, regarding the "pair of the primary and the auxiliary" within the context of *śamatha* (calm abiding) and *vipaśyanā* (insight): the Perfect and Sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is the primary practice, which consists of the twenty-five gates.
If, however, the delusions that obstruct the principle are strong while the efficacy of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* is slight, one must necessarily rely upon the empowerment of divine mantras (*dhāraṇī*).
Thus, there is the three-week construction of the altar. As the Sūtra says: "Furthermore, by means of other skillful expedients (*upāya*), one assists in manifesting the [Truth]."

First, regarding the single principle: because the primary and auxiliary practices proceed together, the attainment of fruition is even more rapid. Seventh, within the context of the primary and auxiliary practices, we speak of the pair of "practice" (gyō) and "stages" (i):
practice possesses the function of advancing toward a goal; that which advances is the three gradual stages, and that which is advanced toward consists of the fifty-five stages.
This is because practice necessarily leads one into these stages. Eighth, within the context of practice and stages, we speak of the pair of "cause" (in) and "result" (ka).

As long as the stages of practice have not reached their ultimate limit, they all belong to the causal mind. Only when bodhi is perfected can it be called the fruition-enlightenment (*phala-bodhi*), for the cause must necessarily result in the fruit.
Ninth, regarding the unity of essence and function within the context of cause and effect: the cause and effect of one's own practice constitute the essence.

The transformation of others through cause and effect constitutes its function; for the essence must necessarily give rise to function. Tenth, regarding the statement that "the six are identical with the one" following the discussion of essence and function:

this is because both self and other possess the meaning of the "six being identical. That is to say, "six" refers to the distinctness of the phenomena of cause and effect, while "identical" reveals the equality of the principle of ordinary beings and sages.
By clarifying the meaning of "six," one avoids giving rise to arrogance; by clarifying the meaning of "identical," one [avoids falling into nihilism].

One may feel despondent; yet, regarding their nature and principle, one knows that the six are always identical, and regarding their cultivation and phenomena, one knows that the identity is always the six.
Thus, what is now called the "Great Buddha-Crown" is the wondrous nature that is neither cause nor fruit.
Śūraṅgama is the wondrous cultivation that penetrates from cause to fruition. Therefore, those who practice for transcendence must first awaken to the principle of the Great Buddha-Crown;
they must realize that the five aggregates, the six sense bases, the twelve bases, and the eighteen elements are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of suchness.
Only then, regarding all phenomena such as the aggregates, bases, and elements, may one, at will, take up any...
There is one dharma: the principle of the perfect three truths—emptiness, conventionality, and the middle—which is none other than suchness itself.

All of these may serve as the object of contemplation. Based on this object, one cultivates contemplation; the wisdom that performs this contemplation is the threefold contemplation within a single mind, also termed the threefold cessation within a single mind.

To illumine the principle of the ultimate truth is the contemplation of emptiness; to illumine the principle of the conventional truth is the contemplation of conventionality; to illumine the principle of the middle truth is [the contemplation of the middle].

The Middle Way contemplation (*madhyamaka-vipaśyanā*) is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), which is the cessation through abiding in the true essence (*tattva-śamatha*). The provisional contemplation (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*) is the cessation through following conditions with skillful means (*upāya-anuvartana-śamatha*).

The Middle Way contemplation is the cessation through quelling the discrimination of the two extremes (*antadvaya-vikalpa-śamatha*). Furthermore, the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) correspond to the contemplation of emptiness, and the three types of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) correspond to the provisional contemplation.

The non-duality of cessation and contemplation is the Middle Way contemplation. In the causal stage, they are called cessation and contemplation; in the resultant stage, they are called concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). This is the efficacy of cessation and contemplation.
It is accomplished; it is named the King of Śūraṅgama, the Wondrous Samādhi. Taking this as its cause, it is named the Secret Cause of the Tathāgata.
By practicing this single path, one fulfills the myriad practices of a Bodhisattva. The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is that which adorns it.
Śūraṅgama: Because it is able to adorn that which is both subject and object as non-dual, it is the "Sublime Adornment.

Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all transcend through this single gate onto the path of sublime adornment. That which fully explains these various meanings is called a *sūtra* (scripture).
That which prefaces and outlines the essential principles is called the "Preface" (*nidāna*). This concludes the combined commentary.

The second part consists of two sections on word-by-word analysis (*nirukti*). First is the analysis of the specific title; second is the analysis of the general title. The first section further contains two parts:
first, the analysis of "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahā-buddhōṣṇīṣa*); second, the analysis of "Śūraṅgama. This is the first [part].

Regarding the three characters of "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" (Dàfódǐng), there are commentaries based on the phenomenal aspect (*shì*) and those based on the principle aspect (*lǐ*). Explanations by masters of past and present fill more than one building;
I have no leisure to record them here. Now, I shall directly elucidate this by means of the single thought-moment of the mind-nature as it manifests before all sentient beings.
The single thought-moment of our present mind is fundamentally not a physical mass of flesh, nor is it a shadow of conditions;
it truly has no spatial dimensions and no boundaries. Therefore, it does not exist within, without, or in between; it has no before or after, nor does it possess temporal duration.
Consequently, it does not belong to the past, present, or future. Yet, this mind is not one among all phenomena.
No phenomena can encompass it, yet this mind is precisely all phenomena; no phenomenon can escape it. It is neither identical to nor distinct from them;
it is both identical and not identical. The path of language is cut off, and the sphere of mental activity ceases.
Having no choice, we forcibly name it "Great. This is not "Great" spoken in contrast to "Small"; were it "Great" spoken in contrast to "Small," then the Great would have limits.

[This is] not a measure, for it is not a truly finite magnitude. Nor does it become large after first being small; if it were small first and then large, that magnitude would have a beginning and an end, and thus would not be inherently great.
In sum, it is inexhaustible throughout the ten directions and unfathomable across the three periods of time; therefore, it is called "Great. This greatness has three meanings:

first, the meaning of transcending faults and severing non-virtue, which is the Greatness of Essence (*tattva-mahat*); second, vertical pervasiveness through time and horizontal pervasiveness through space.
The "Meaning" (yi) is precisely the Great Aspect (xiang-da). Third, it is fully endowed with meanings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; this is the Great Function (yong-da).
Because the single thought-moment of our present mind is spiritually luminous and unobscured, clearly and constantly aware, it is called "Buddha. "Buddha" means awakening.

Awakening (*jue*) has three meanings. First, the meaning of perfect clarity and solitary illumination; this is self-awakening (*zizhào*). Second, the meaning of illuminating and comprehending in accordance with conditions; this is awakening through others (*tazhào*).
Third, the meaning of penetrating illumination of the source of the mind; this is full awakening (*manzhào*).

Because the single thought-moment of our present mind is immeasurable and boundless in its extent, and its essence is supremely honored and infinite, it is called the "Crown" (*ding*). The Crown has three meanings. First—

First is the meaning of supreme honor, for all dharmas cannot be compared to it. Second is the meaning of being invisible, for it is entirely free from the four errors and transcends all hundred negations.
Third is the meaning of emitting light and manifesting transformations, for it responds universally according to conditions without being defiled by any dust.
One character contains these three meanings; each of the three contains nine. If analyzed in detail, the meanings should be immeasurable.
The immeasurable and wondrous meanings are, in essence, but this single mind. Therefore, it is said that the single mind constitutes the Great Buddha-Crown (Mahā-uṣṇīṣa).
This is the inherent virtue of the nature of sentient beings, the primary substance of the present sutra, and furthermore, the substance of all Mahayana sutras.
Since all the temporal teachings of a lifetime expounded by the Tathāgata are discourses that accord with the true nature (dharmatā), it is called "Buddha."
To say that the teachings of the higher and lower vehicles are produced solely by this one mind—to speak thus is called the correct teaching;

if one speaks otherwise, it is the speech of Pāpīyān. Furthermore, if one can awaken to the meaning of this Great Buddha-Crown, one will be able to penetrate the wondrous meaning of the entire scripture.
Herein, I shall not avoid prolixity but shall extract its essential pivot and provide a brief elucidation.
The Sūtra begins with Ānanda requesting the initial expedient means for *śamatha*, *samādhi*, and *dhyāna*.

To realize the meaning of the Great [Vehicle] is the expedient means of *dhyāna*; to realize the meaning of the Buddha is the expedient means of *śamatha*; to realize the meaning of the Summit is the expedient means of *samādhi*.
Furthermore, the greatness of essence is the expedient means of *dhyāna*; the greatness of characteristics is... [the expedient means of *samādhi*].
The expedient means of *śamatha* is vast; this is the expedient means of *samādhi*.
Furthermore, *śamatha* is self-awakening, *samādhi* is awakening through others, and *dhyāna* is perfect awakening. Moreover, *dhyāna* is the most honored;
*śamatha* is invisible, while *samādhi* emits light and manifests transformations. Furthermore, the three are one, which is *śamatha*; the one is...
The three are samādhi; they are neither one nor three, yet they are both three and one. This is dhyāna.

Furthermore, it is the essence of the eternally abiding true mind, which is pure and luminous by nature. Its luminosity by nature is śamatha, which corresponds to the greatness of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-mahattva). Its purity by nature is samādhi.

That which is the Great Function is the eternally abiding *dhyāna*; that which is the Great Essence consists of the three [aspects] of each of the Buddha’s Usnīṣas, extending even to the three within one and the one within three—neither one nor three, yet three and one, as explained above in the section on the "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Locations."

The direct refutation that the seven locations are all non-existent is the greatness of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahattva*). The indirect demonstration that the seven locations are all existent is the greatness of their function (*vṛtti-mahattva*).

The samādhi named Śūraṅgama-rāja is the greatness of their essence (*svabhāva-mahattva*). Regarding the three [aspects] for each of the one hundred and one [locations], up to the Buddha-crests, each has three;
these are as explained above. Within the text that analyzes the seeing in ten sections, each section contains this meaning, which is now abbreviated here.

The second and third [aspects] are: the subject together with emptiness is the greatness of characteristic (*lakṣaṇamahat*), and the guest together with the objects of sense is the greatness of function (*karmamahat*);
both are devoid of dual nature, which is the greatness of essence (*svabhāvamahat*). Pointing to all these as things, there is no "seer," which is the greatness of characteristic;
subtly illuminating them, there is nothing that is not the seer, which is the greatness of function. This is fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. How could it be...?
That which exists within [this] as "is" and "is not" is the Greatness of Essence (*tattva-mahat*).
That the seeing and its conditions, along with the perceived forms, are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent, is the Greatness of Characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*).

That this is originally the wondrously luminous, unsurpassed Bodhi—the pure, perfect, true mind—which through delusion manifests as form and emptiness, as well as hearing and seeing, is the Greatness of Function (*vṛtti-mahat*). This seeing and its conditions are originally Bodhi.
To extract the essence of wondrous, pure, and luminous substance is the "Greatness of Substance" (ti-da). [The three sets of three, up to the Buddha-Usnīṣa, each having three, are as explained above.

Within the four sections of the text, to seek within the true, eternal nature for coming and going, delusion and awakening, birth and death, and find nothing at all, is the "Greatness of Characteristic" (xiang-da).
That which is illusory and false is called "characteristic"; this is the "Greatness of Function" (yong-da). Its nature is truly the wondrous enlightenment.
The clarity of the essence is the greatness of essence (*tài-dà*). Within the seven points of greatness, "pervading the dharma-realm" is the greatness of characteristics (*xiàng-dà*).
"Inherent form is true emptiness; inherent emptiness is true form; they manifest according to karma" is the greatness of function (*yòng-dà*). "Pure and fundamentally so" is the greatness of essence.

In the *Dazhong yuanwu wen* (The Great Assembly’s Perfect Enlightenment Text), it says: "The mind pervades the ten directions; being empty like a leaf or a blade of grass, this is the greatness of aspect (*xiàngdà*).

The physical body born of one's parents is like a speck of dust or a bubble; this is the greatness of function (*yòngdà*). Objects are the wondrous mind, and the essence of mind contains and envelops all; this is the greatness of substance (*tǐdà*).
All three Tathāgata-garbhas are simultaneously 'not'—this is the greatness of aspect. All are simultaneously 'are'—this is the greatness of function."
"Detached from both 'is' and 'is not'; it is both 'is' and 'is not. This is the Greatness of Essence (*tattva-mahātmya*)," which is the object of contemplation for each of the twenty-five gates.

Each one possesses the threefold reality of perfect, pervasive, and common; this is the Perfect Reality (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*). "This is the Greatness of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-mahātmya*)," which is the Pervasive Reality (*samvṛti-tattva*).
It is the Great Function. It is eternally real; it is the Great Essence. The fivefold assembly’s divine mantra is named *Mahāsāttvapatrā*.
This translates as "Great White Parasol. "White" is the Great Characteristic; "Parasol" is the Great Function; "Mahā" is the Great Essence.
Regarding the sixty noble stages, in the third section on the gradual sequence, it says: "All Tathāgatas..."

The secret, the perfect, the pure, and the wondrous all manifest within it. "Perfect" refers to the greatness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇamahattva*); "pure" refers to the greatness of function (*karmamahattva*); and "secret" refers to the greatness of essence (*svabhāvamahattva*).
It is neither three nor one, yet it is both three and one; that these three and one are both inconceivable is called "wondrous.

The triad of one and one, and the triad of three, even extending to the three at each of the Buddha’s cranial protuberances, are all as described above. This is a brief indication of the general purport of the entire text.
End. Second, the explanation of *Śūraṅgama*.
The three characters *Śūraṅgama* directly point to the concentration of nature (*xingding*) wherein all practitioners give rise to cultivation based entirely upon their inherent nature. This is...
This is an abbreviated name for the Great Samādhi. In full, it should be called the *Mahābuddhāloka-śūraṅgama-rāja*.
*Śūraṅgama* means that all phenomena (*dharma*) are ultimately firm and solid.

Here, the term "all phenomena" refers in total to the root-bodies and the environmental worlds of the ten dharma-realms—namely, the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve spheres (*dhātu*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The "elements" (dhātu) refer to the seven great elements. As for the phrase "ultimately firm and solid": "ultimate" means thorough and fundamental;
"firm and solid" means eternally abiding. This refers to having reached the very source of all phenomena, being unmoving and indestructible.
The meaning is that once a practitioner has awakened to the nature of the Great Buddha-Crown, they are able to fully realize that one nature is all natures, and all natures are one nature.
Therefore, among all phenomena—the aggregates (*skandhas*), bases (*āyatanas*), and elements (*dhātus*)—there is not a single one that is not the nature of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
Thus it is said: "The fundamental Tathāgatagarbha is the wondrous true suchness-nature. As the Sūtra says:

"All conditions of form and mind, as well as the mental factors (*caitta*) and their objects, are manifested solely by the mind. Your body, your mind, and externally the mountains, rivers, and empty space [are likewise so]."
The great earth is entirely a manifestation within the wondrously functioning true essence, the wondrous mind; it is merely an object appearing therein.

One must understand that the entirety of nature gives rise to cultivation, and naturally, the entirety of cultivation resides within nature; there is no cultivation apart from nature. This is because nature has nothing external to it.
Furthermore, regarding this very method of cultivation, one should still grasp the subtle purport of practice found within the sutras.
It is said that by practicing based on the ultimate emptiness of all phenomena, one accomplishes the *śamatha* samādhi of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

By practicing based on the ultimate conventionality, one accomplishes the *samāpatti* samādhi of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). By practicing based on the ultimate middle way, one accomplishes the *dhyāna* samādhi of the middle truth (*madhya-satya*).
Furthermore, the three being one is the samādhi of the ultimate truth; the one being three is the [samādhi of] the conventional truth.
The Samādhi of the Truths is neither one nor three; yet it is both three and one.

Within this Samādhi of the Truths, the three and the one are perfectly interfused, and for this reason it is called "Wondrous. This single samādhi encompasses all samādhis; therefore, it is termed the King of Śūraṅgama Samādhis.
The samādhis cultivated by the twenty-five sages are precisely this samādhi of the perfect interfusion of the three and the one.
Indeed, this is because the Dharma-gates are equal by nature, originally devoid of superiority or inferiority.
Furthermore, that Mañjuśrī singled out the ear-door as the most excellent was intended for a specific class of practitioners at that time, desiring that they follow the path back home;
it was not out of any partiality toward Avalokiteśvara. Generally speaking, once a Great Being who has realized the mind has awakened to the nature of the Great Buddha-Usnīsa, he must...
One is able to thoroughly comprehend the nature of equality of all phenomena.

Therefore, whichever phenomenon one selects, it may all serve as the object of contemplation, for each possesses the three meanings of perfection, universality, and the ultimate reality. This is not true only of Avalokiteśvara;
those engaged in the study of wisdom must know this. For this reason, I have previously remarked that Master Lingfeng Xu [classified]...

"Study" here refers to the Hīnayāna. To say that one "transcends by a finger-snap" intends to reveal that through this sutra, one attains the Dharma-body without passing through the *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*.
If the deluded mind ceases, that cessation is itself Bodhi; thus, one may suddenly transcend the limited fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.

The statement that the ease of attaining the Way is like the duration of a finger-snap is the "Supreme Sentence," which precisely reveals the reason for its unique excellence; this constitutes the Introduction.

The Master investigated the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma across five periods. If one were to say that this scripture, which universally encompasses those with the capacity for transformation and directly points to the essence of mind,
even enabling people to transcend all at once by a mere snap of the fingers and attain Buddhahood on the spot—
there is nothing more sublime than this sutra.
Third, the clarification of names, meanings, causes, and effects.
To explain its name: "The Ultimate Firmness of All Phenomena" refers to that which penetrates the very source of all dharmas—unmoving and indestructible.
It is from this that the secret cause of the Tathāgata and the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas derive their beginning, and to which they ultimately return.

It is simply this. The first phrase clarifies the name; "explanation" (*śāstra*) means to interpret. As for "its name," it refers specifically to *Śūraṅgama*, which is translated as "the ultimate solidity of all phenomena," as explained in the title.
The second phrase explains the meaning; that is, the sense of the most vital point. Regarding "that which... [the text continues].

"Shuo" (said) refers to what has been expounded. To "trace the source" (*yuan qi shuo*) means to provide an exegesis that advances the understanding. "Che" (penetrating) signifies the state of thorough and clear awakening.

"Fa" (dharmas) points to all phenomena, referring to the meaning of their intrinsic nature as the basis for maintenance. The two characters "di" (bottom/foundation) and "yuan" (source) both refer to the eternally abiding true mind.
Because the mind serves as the support for all things, it is called the "foundation. All dharmas arise from... [the source].
Because the mind manifests [all things], it is called the "source" (*yuan*). To be unmoving and indestructible is the meaning of being eternally abiding and unchanging.

What is now termed "penetrating" (*che*) refers to the thorough illumination that all phenomena are solely mind; that phenomena abide in their own positions, and that the characteristics of the world are eternal.
The single word "phenomenon" (*fa*) explains the meaning of all things; being unmoving and indestructible explains ultimate solidity.
Regarding the meaning: the title of this sutra, *Śūraṅgama*, refers to what the ancient masters called "thoroughly reaching the source of all phenomena—unmoving and indestructible.

From the passage beginning with "And the Tathāgata... onwards, it correctly clarifies that from the causal stage through to the fruition, there is nothing that does not exhaust these eight characters.
The word "而" (*ér*) is a particle used for prosodic flow; it is also a term used for slight transitions. It is not a textual error.
The character "er" (而) means that the blood vessels are obstructed. "Tathāgata" refers to one who has attained the fruit; "bodhisattvas" refers to those on the path of cause.
"Secret cause" refers to the cause; these are the three causes of Buddha-nature. This nature is precisely the single thought-moment of our own present consciousness.
The aforementioned "that which is without movement or destruction" is the direct cause (*hetu-bhūta*) of Buddhahood, the Buddha-nature;

the previously mentioned "awakening to the fact that all phenomena are mind-only"—the word "awakening" (*bodhi*)—is the completing cause (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*) of Buddhahood, the Buddha-nature. This extends even to such acts as raising a hand or lowering the head.
The various kinds of wholesome practices are the causal conditions for attaining Buddhahood; the Buddha-nature is the Tathāgata’s ultimate fruit;
and the Sage is the perfected state—these alone constitute my three causes. Because sentient beings are deluded and do not know this, it is called "esoteric" (*mi*).
The myriad practices are the causal conditions for attaining Buddhahood. "Myriad" (*wan*) is a general number in this context, signifying their great abundance.
These practices for cultivating virtue are collectively termed two kinds: namely, meritorious action (*puṇya-karma*) and wisdom-action (*jñāna-karma*).

When one speaks of the bodhisattva’s practice of benefiting self and others, traversing the stages (*bhūmi*) to cultivate them, such practices should be immeasurable. For instance, in the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), one plants the seeds of Buddhahood by fully developing the faculties and powers;

in the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), one is born into the Buddha-family and becomes a son of the Buddha; and in the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), one extensively cultivates the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*).
Performing the Buddha-work: the ten dedications turn the Buddha-work toward the Buddha-mind; the four stages of application merge with the Buddha-mind and extinguish all numerical distinctions;
the ten grounds accord with True Suchness and encompass Nirvana; Equal Enlightenment aligns with the limit of Buddhahood and shatters the mark of birth.
Each contains all others; principal and satellites are mutually interpenetrating; dependent origination is unimpeded, like the pearls of Indra’s net, reflecting and illuminating one another.
It is inexhaustible. The present mention of "ten thousand" merely serves to manifest the vastness of its number.
"Mǐ" means "none"; "zī" means "to receive" or "to be endowed with"; "shǐ" means "the beginning. This term refers directly to the ever-present true mind of the present moment.
The meaning is that when Bodhisattvas first resolve their minds to cultivate the causes of enlightenment, there is nothing that does not receive its endowment from this.

Regarding the mind: that which returns to the ultimate limit refers to the point where one has finally and perfectly attained the fruit of Buddhahood, yet returns once more to this very mind as the ultimate limit.

This consists of two parts: first, clarifying principle and practice; second, clarifying nature and cultivation. Now, for the first part: clarifying principle and practice. *Note: The term "four Ming" (四明) likely refers to the teachings of the lineage of Zhiyi (Tiantai), specifically the school of Zhili (Zhili of the Four Ming Temples).*
Examining that which is expressed, one finds it discusses the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna*) to clarify true nature, and opens up the perfect practice to demonstrate true cultivation.
Examining the meaning of "investigation" (*vicaya*) and "thorough analysis" (*pravicaya*), the term "pointing to things" refers specifically to this very scripture.

To say that words can manifest the principle is called "expression"; thus, the written characters are the "expresser" (*vācaka*), and the wondrous principle is the "expressed" (*vācya*). This is the essential point of the preceding discourse.

"Words" (*ci*) refers to discourse and proclamation. "Perfect" (*yuan*) refers to the perfectly interfused Middle Way. "Principle" (*li*) refers to the principle of equality. "Clarity" (*ming*) refers to clear awakening.
The two characters "True Nature" (*zhenxing*) point directly to the wondrous mind inherently possessed by all of us.

This mind has never been false, hence it is called "True"; it remains unchanged through all time, hence it is called "Nature. The meaning of this phrase is that the author of the preface consulted the preceding three [sections].
The textual content of this fascicle exclusively discusses the principle of the perfectly interfused Middle Way; hence it is called "that which is expounded.

It universally causes all sentient beings to individually awaken to and clarify that their own minds are inherently endowed [with all virtues], serving as the foundation for cultivation and practice. Thus it is said: "Opening..."
"Manifesting" means revealing; "practicing" means cultivating. To initiate practice based on the perfect principle is called "perfect practice" (*yuánxíng*);

to initiate cultivation from true nature is called "true cultivation" (*zhēnxiū*). True nature is an alternative name for the perfect principle, and true cultivation is an alternative name for perfect practice.
"Manifesting" refers to pointing out, meaning that one should consult the scriptures from fascicle four through fascicle eight.
As for "elucidation," it is entirely for the purpose of revealing and demonstrating how to give rise to perfect practice based on the principle of the dependent and the perfected,
so that the practitioner may initiate true cultivation from true nature.
Second, the clarification of nature and cultivation.

As for its nature, both essence and function are simultaneously manifested. As for its cultivation, cause and fruit are unified in a single accord. Examining the beginning and tracing back to the end—this is the teaching of definitive meaning.
"Its nature" refers to the true nature mentioned above; "its cultivation" refers to the true cultivation mentioned above. These are the two.

The term "character" (*zi*) refers to its employment within the context of sentences and phrases; it is not a word used for a pause. Rather, it signifies the essential substance of falling back down and then rising again.

This is the principle of immutability. "Employment" (*yòng*) refers to the phenomena that follow conditions. To say they "manifest together" (*shuang chāng*): "manifest" (*chāng*) means to reveal or make clear.
The meaning is this: that which is called "nature" (dharmatā) here is neither the nature-reason of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*), nor is it the Buddha-nature of the mere-middle (*kevala-madhyama*).
It does not lack the possession of all phenomena; rather, this nature is the nature-reason of the perfectly interfused Middle Way (*pariniṣpanna-madhyamā-pratipad*), wherein one possesses all.
Therefore, throughout the first three fascicles of the sutra, the principle is revealed through phenomena, and the nature is elucidated through characteristics.
Therefore, it is said that both essence and function are manifested together. Regarding "the fruition and the cause are unified": "fruition" refers to the awakening of the fruition;
"cause" refers to the causal mind. "Unified" means they are in perfect accord.

The meaning is that what is called "cultivation" here is not the cultivation of ordinary or inferior beings with a mind of birth and extinction, nor is it the cultivation of the provisional vehicles that remains detached from the two extremes. This cultivation is, rather, preceded by the realization of the perfect principle.

Subsequently, one practices with perfect cultivation: practicing one thing is to practice all things; when the cause encompasses the fruit and the fruit reaches its full penetration, this is called "one accord.

The final phrase serves as a concluding clarification. "Tracing the origin" means investigating the meaning of the beginning; "reaching the end" means harmonizing with the meaning of the conclusion. "Understanding the definitive meaning" (*nītārtha*):

"meaning" refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of one's own mind; "understanding" means being free from concealment. The intent is that one thoroughly investigates the beginning and end within the sutras.
The essential point is this: these are truly the words of the ultimate perfection of the Mahāyāna. First, they shatter false attachments to reveal the true mind;

they harmonize the four categories of phenomena and integrate the seven elements. They clarify the causes of continuity and demonstrate the principle of perfect interfusion, fully manifesting the three collections of the teachings.
Without departing from the one mind, it reveals the inherent virtues of nature so that people may recognize their own minds and not seek them elsewhere.

Within this, two meanings are clarified, the six sense faculties are stabilized, and the various methods of perfect penetration are set forth; it demonstrates the reality and points toward the true path to Bodhi.
It enables people to find the gate and enter the chamber, to set out on the path and return home.
Subsequently, one employs the precepts and karma to empty the emotional attachments of the seven realms of existence, and cultivates meditative concentration to break the cage of the five aggregates.
Eventually, one perfects Bodhi and completes all that must be done. Is this not, indeed, the ultimate, clearly manifest teaching, free from all hidden ambiguities?
The two prefaces consist of six sections regarding the text and its meaning. First, the preface concerning the response of the capacity; second, the preface concerning the arising of the teaching;

third, the revelation of the perfect principle; fourth, the demonstration of the perfect practice; fifth, the elucidation of the perfect realization; sixth, the conclusion of the perfect name. Now, the first [section].
This is truly because practitioners turn their backs on the truth and head toward delusion, failing to achieve unsurpassed Bodhi;
or they cherish the Lesser Vehicle and consider a small attainment sufficient; or they fail to eliminate the outflows of desire, allowing their learning to become a source of fault.

This section offers a general praise for those on the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*). It laments that they fail to awaken to the perfect principle (*pariniṣpanna-tattva*) and, instead of practicing correctly, enter onto deviant paths;
this is not the fault of the Dharma-gate. The phrase "it is truly due to" (*liáng yóu zhě*) expresses a sigh of certainty and beyond doubt.

"All practitioners" refers generally to the seven types of expedient means, namely: Bodhisattvas of the three teachings, as well as those of the *śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha* vehicles of the *āgama* and *vaipulya* [teachings], and so forth.

Ordinary beings, followers of external paths, Māra, and his retinue were all originally practitioners who turned their backs on the True—meaning they opposed it—and turned toward the False—meaning they followed it.
"True" refers to the One True Dharma-realm, the wondrous mind inherently present; "False" refers to the shadowy reflections of the six sense-objects and the marks of arising and ceasing thoughts.
That we now speak of turning one's back on the True and turning toward the False clearly points to the perversion of sentient beings.
This refers to the performance of practices. "Unsurpassed Bodhi" is an alternative designation for the fruit of Buddhahood. "Not accomplished" means being unable to achieve it.
The meaning is that sentient beings resolve their minds and practice cultivation originally for the sake of achieving the fruit of Buddhahood;

to say instead that they do not accomplish it is due to the fault of turning one's back on the truth and heading toward delusion, performing practices in a state of inverted perception. The following two phrases point to...
"Passing over" or "exceeding" is an indefinite term. "Diligently not abandoning" is called *āśaya* (love/affection). The constant movement of the mind is called *smṛti* (mindfulness/thought).
"Vehicle" (*yāna*) has the meaning of "carrying and transporting. "Hīnayāna" refers to the two vehicles of the Lesser Teaching. Regarding the phrase "taking little as sufficient":

"little" means a small portion, clarifying the sense of limitation; "sufficient" means to be fully satisfied. The meaning of this sentence is that [this applies to] the two vehicles of the Lesser Teaching.

It is like the carts of sheep or deer; they can only benefit oneself and cannot deliver others. Originally, one seeks to transcend the three realms out of weariness with the suffering of birth and death.
Once one has attained emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), one then cherishes these states at every thought-moment.
Believing that because of diligent exertion within the Buddha-dharma one has obtained much and reached the ultimate fulfillment, it is therefore said that "one has attained."

"Little is enough. Regarding "the outflows of desire (*kāma-āsrava*) not being eliminated": there are three fundamental outflows, namely the outflow of desire, the outflow of existence (*bhava-āsrava*), and the outflow of ignorance (*avidyā-āsrava*).

To eliminate the outflow of desire is to transcend the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*); to eliminate the outflow of existence is to transcend the three realms; to eliminate the outflow of ignorance is to be free from the three [formless] emptinesses.

"Accumulation" (*saṃcaya*) means to nurture or harbor; "fault" (*doṣa*) means transgression. To say that "accumulating learning becomes a fault" refers to hearing that constitutes the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).

At the very beginning of establishing the foundation, if one hears the Dharma and practices it, this is precisely the supreme path of cultivation—namely, hearing and reflecting, reflecting and practicing, and practicing and realizing.
What fault could there be in this? That it is now said to constitute a fault is due to the underlying ailment of "hoarding" (or "accumulation").

This means that upon hearing the Dharma, one is unwilling to contemplate the mind; one does not strive for true cultivation or actual realization, but merely follows the dust of sensory objects and discriminative thought, allowing the mind to flow away in distraction.

The sound of rushing [words]. Even if one hears the profound meaning of the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*) in the Mahāyāna sūtras for a lifetime, it only increases the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of names and words;
because one follows along with the flow of sensory objects, it is said that "the outflows of desire are not eliminated.

Because one merely calculates upon profound expressions and wondrous phrases, it is said that "accumulating learning becomes a fault. That the Tathāgata calls such a person "one who is to be pitied" is truly lamentable.
The section on the Response of the Capacity is concluded.
Part Two: The Preface to the Arising of the Teaching. Three sections: First, skillfully demonstrating the causal origination; second, pointing out the eternal mind;
third, pre-emptively indicating the fixed title. Now, the first.
Therefore, Ānanda took extensive learning and improper attachment as conditions to extensively propagate the Great Teaching.

This section clarifies that while one may hear the teachings, failing to practice them leads to the accumulation of faults through mere learning; this serves as a cautionary tale for the study of wisdom (*prajñā*).
In Sanskrit, Ānanda means "Joyous Celebration" (*Prīti-nandana*). Among the Buddha’s disciples, he was foremost in extensive learning. As for "improper attachment," it refers to...
The Venerable One went on his alms round in regular succession. This was due to the incident involving the seduction by Sundarī. "On account of this" (*etad-vaśāt*) means "by reason of this";
it signifies the depth [of the cause]. "The Great Teaching" refers to the present sutra. The use of the character "yòng" (用) is a term used to connect what precedes with what follows.

To say it "connects with what precedes" means that since the previous passage stated that possessing extensive learning could lead to transgression, the Venerable One thus had the conditions for falling [into error]; this is intended to clarify [the following point].
Even those who have accumulated the merit of extensive learning over many kalpas cannot yet avoid the occurrence of deviant attachments;
how much less can one who is now a beginner, having only just entered the lecture hall, be called a man of the Way? Those who study wisdom today should reflect in this manner.

Regarding the phrase "arousing the inferior," this refers to the Great Teaching of this sutra. If it were not for the demonstration of falling [into lower realms], there would be no way to initiate [the teaching].

What are called "evil causes and conditions" are, in fact, "wholesome causes and conditions. This is the profound compassionate vow of the Venerable One; how could it be anything other than a manifestation of great skillful means?
Therefore, it is said: "Profoundly arousing the Great Teaching. The Introductory Section (Nidāna) is concluded. Below follows the Main Body (Saddharma).
Second, he points out the eternally abiding mind.

The World-Honored One first addressed him, saying: "The continuous succession of birth and death for all sentient beings arises entirely from their failure to know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of nature that is pure and luminous.
By employing various false thoughts, and because these thoughts are not real, there is cyclic wandering."

This section is the crux of the entire sutra; it is the secret method for shattering delusion. Because the true mind of sentient beings has been sealed and confined by ignorance, it cannot manifest of its own accord.
Now, as the World-Honored One intends to shatter delusion and reveal the truth for the sake of sentient beings, he first pierces through it with a single word.
The first to be addressed was Ānanda, who saw the Buddha and made his request.
"Please come later. These were the words the Buddha first spoke as a preliminary instruction. There are nine types of sentient beings, namely the three sages and the six ordinary beings.

There are two kinds of birth and death: first, transformation; second, segmented. There are three kinds of delusive thoughts: first, ignorance (*avidyā*); second, dust-sand-like afflictions; third, views and thoughts.
There are three modes of transmigration: first, transmigration in the realm of true recompense; second, transmigration through skillful means; third, [transmigration in the realm of shared reward].

While we dwell together in the cycle of saṃsāra, the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of purity and luminosity—is precisely the nature of the single thought-moment of our present consciousness.
This mind is quiescent yet ever-illuminating; this is called the "luminous nature. It is illuminating yet ever-quiescent; this is called the "pure nature.

Being both quiescent and illuminating, it undergoes no change from antiquity to the present; this is called "eternally abiding. To be deluded regarding this one mind is to be in the midst of birth and death.
When one awakens to the single mind, saṃsāra ceases instantaneously. What is now called "continuity" precisely clarifies that from time immemorial one has never awakened;
therefore, it is said that one "does not know. This "not knowing" refers to the absence of the power of wisdom-illumination.
Because one does not know that the mind is eternally abiding, one employs ignorance and delusive thought. Because one does not know that the nature of the mind is pure, one employs...
Because of the delusions as numerous as motes of dust, one does not know that the nature of the mind is luminous; thus, one employs the delusions of views and thoughts.
Because these delusions of ignorance are not true, there is the cycle of transformation and death within the *sambhoga-kāya* (recompense) land.
Because these delusions as numerous as motes of dust are not true, there is the cycle of transformation and death within the *upāya-kāya* (expedient) land. These [delusions of] views and thoughts...
Because false conceptualization is not true, there is the cycle of birth-and-death through segmented existence within the Land of Common Dwelling.
Third, the fixed name is revealed:
furthermore, it is said that there is a samādhi named the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, which fully encompasses the ten thousand practices throughout the ten directions.
The Tathāgata’s single gate is the path of wondrous adornment that transcends all; is this not indeed the fundamental basis for both principle and practice in this sutra?
This section constitutes the very core of the sutra and serves as a marvelous remedy for sentient beings to cure the disease of birth and death.
The phrase "it is further said" refers to the Buddha’s words of repeated instruction. In Sanskrit, it is *samādhi*, also called *samāpatti*;
in Chinese, it is translated as "right reception" (*zhèngshòu*), meaning that one does not receive the various sensory objects (*viṣaya*).

It is also called "right concentration" (*zhèngdìng*), meaning that it is neither the instability of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) nor the false concentration of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The term "king" (*wáng*) carries the sense of universal governance; it refers to this single *samādhi*.
Because it is able to encompass all samādhis, its name is the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King.
"To be fully endowed with ten thousand practices" means that by cultivating this single practice of samādhi, one is able to perfectly include and encompass all practices.
Regarding the phrase "the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend through a single gate": "gate" (*mukha*) means "passage. Samādhi is that which enables passage;

the fruit of Buddhahood and Bodhi is that which is passed through. The meaning is that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions, originally starting from the stage of ordinary beings, cultivated this single practice of samādhi and thereby transcended the two oceans of birth and death through this one gate, passing through fifty... [kalpas].
The five stages are the true path to Bodhi; one ascends directly to the shore of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment.

As for the "Path of Wondrous Adornment," the Dharma-body is that which is adorned, and samādhi is that which performs the adornment; the non-duality of nature and cultivation constitutes "wondrous adornment.
This refers to the *Mahā-buddha-uṣṇīṣa*, the fundamental principle of this single sūtra, and the *Śūraṅgama*, the [title] of this single sūtra.
It is the root of practice. Therefore, we know that this very King of Samādhis is indeed the fundamental basis for both the principle and the practice throughout this entire sutra.
The two characters "ye ye" (也耶) are words of sighing and admiration uttered by Xu Xie. This concludes the section on the arising of the teaching.

The third [section] reveals the perfect principle in four parts: first, a detailed examination and inquiry into the mind and the discernment of vision, which serves to destroy the false and reveal the true;

second, an extensive listing of the four categories and seven great points to clarify that total delusion is itself truth; third, answering objections regarding the attachment to characteristics to resolve the non-duality of nature and characteristics;
fourth, citing the pursuit of delusion while losing sight of truth to show that delusion has no fundamental cause. Regarding the first [part]:
Second: First, the introduction concerning the investigation of the mind through seven locations; second, the introduction concerning the discernment of vision through ten rounds. Now, for the first:
by means of this, the clinging to the seven locations is refuted, and two distinct types of fundamental [ignorance] are distinguished.

The first phrase correctly sequences the inquiry into the mind. The two characters "yóu shì" (thereby) serve as transitional terms that follow from the preceding text and lead into the subsequent text.

Since the initial meaning was already introduced in the previous section—where the compassionate concern of teacher and disciple served as the catalyst for the Great Teaching—the present seven locations are directly derived from that preceding text;
hence, it says "yóu shì. "Pān" means to grasp or seize; "yuán" means to condition or rely upon.
The "object" (*viṣaya*) is that which is grasped; the "grasping" (*ālambana*) is that which grasps. The grasper is the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses;

the grasped is the image-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses. Both the seeing and image divisions arise illusorily from the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses and possess no substantial reality.
Fundamentally, they cannot be destroyed; it is only because sentient beings do not understand that the seeing and image divisions are illusory that [confusion arises]. When...

The essence consists of the self-cognizing part (*svasaṃvedana-bhāga*) and the self-cognized part (*svasaṃvitti-saṃvedana-bhāga*), yet one falsely discriminates the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) as the mind and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as form, grasping them as substantially existent.
Therefore, false conceptions arise regarding [the mind] being internal, external, or even all such non-attached [positions].
Thus, the Buddha refuted these by showing that they are not valid in any of the seven locations; this was intended to reveal that there is no location among these seven that is not [ultimately] so.
Regarding the distinction between these two fundamental natures, the Sūtra says: "The first is the root of beginningless birth and death;
it is that which you and all sentient beings now take as your own nature—the mind of grasping at objects. The second is the original, pure essence of beginningless bodhi and nirvāṇa;
it is that which you now possess as the fundamentally luminous essence of consciousness, capable of giving rise to all conditions."

As for "that which is distinguished": this intends to clarify that one is the source of delusion and the other is the source of truth. "Distinguished" (*bie*) carries the sense of clear and analytical discernment.
Because sentient beings do not understand that both the true and the deluded lack intrinsic nature—that very nature which lacks intrinsic nature is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Now, when we speak of "distinction," it is because the continuous succession of the birth and death of sentient beings arises entirely from their failure to know the Truth.
The mind employs various delusive thoughts, yet it has never been explicitly stated that truth and delusion are without self-nature and are but the single mind.
Now, this is further clarified; therefore, it is said to be "distinct."
Part Two: Distinguishing the Ten Instances of Views. First, a general presentation of the mutual manifestation of mind and views;
second, a detailed enumeration of the ten instances of subtle discernment.

Regarding the first: by means of the view, the mind is manifested; by means of the mind, the view is manifested. Although mind and view manifest each other, the primary manifestation lies in the mind.
"Causes" (yin) means "reliance. That which has form and cannot be hidden is called "seeing" (jian). That which knows all phenomena without exception is called "mind" (xin).
All sentient beings know only that the eyes on their faces can see and the mind within their chests can know.

But how do they know that the faculty of seeing is not necessarily located on the face, and that the faculty of knowing does not necessarily reside within the chest? Furthermore, there are two [aspects].
In their location, they exist neither in being nor in non-being. Now, the Buddha accords with the habitual attachments of sentient beings;
thus, he does not explicitly state whether there is knowing or not knowing, or presence and absence.

He simply uses the mutual illumination of the mind and the eye, saying that "through the mind, seeing is manifested; through seeing, the mind is manifested. This hidden intent precisely reveals that the physical eye has no seeing.

The mind that perceives reflected images is not true cognition; nor does it clearly and explicitly reveal [the truth] so as to cause one to personally realize that former attachments are entirely non-existent.

Only then can one believe that seeing and knowing are fundamentally not two separate things. Therefore, although within this state both mind and seeing manifest each other, the primary manifestation lies in the mind itself.
Second, there are ten distinct sections of exquisite analysis.
For example, the analogy of a blind person staring into the dark illustrates that seeing is not the eye;
this first analysis establishes that the nature of seeing is not the eye. Following this pattern, the phrasing employs the sense of metaphorical extension. "Blind" [is used here figuratively].
A person whose eyes lack luster cannot see objects clearly. "Zhù" (矚) means to look. "Àn" (暗) refers to an environment that is not bright. To explain the meaning:
as for seeing that which is not the eye—everyone has traditionally known only the eyes on their faces as being the faculty of seeing.
Now, suddenly hearing that seeing is not the eye, who could believe it? Therefore, the Buddha pointed to a blind man to illustrate this.
"The darkness seen by the eyes [of one born blind] and the darkness seen by a person with sight when staying in a dark room without the sun, moon, or lamps—are they the same or different?
Ānanda replied, "When comparing these two types of blackness, there is never any difference between them.
The Buddha said, "Suppose that person who was blind suddenly regains their visual faculty and sees various forms; would this be the same as a person with sight obtaining a lamp?"
"Is the seeing of form the same as or different [from the eye]? He replied, "It is not different. The Buddha said: "If a blind person obtains eyes and sees forms, it is called 'seeing with the eyes.
By that same logic, when a person with eyes uses a lamp to see forms, it should be called 'seeing with the lamp.
Therefore, one should know that while the lamp can reveal the form, the seer is not the lamp. By this analogy, the eye can reveal the form, but the seer is not the eye."
"Bending the fingers to track the passing light" serves as a verification for seeing that the nature of seeing is immovable;
this is the second point, distinguishing the immovability of the nature of seeing. "Bending" (qu) means to curve. "Fingers" (zhǐ) refers to the five wheels of the Buddha’s hand.
"Bending the fingers" means to curl and clench them into a fist. A sutra states: "The Tathāgata, in the midst of the great assembly, bent his five wheel-fingers;
having bent them, he opened them again; having opened them, he bent them again.

"Flying light" refers to the Buddha emitting a single jewel-light from the palms of his wheels, which traveled to Ānanda’s side, moving left and right. This serves as a test, meaning a formal interrogation, because Ānanda had witnessed it.
The Buddha’s fingers opened and bent, and light flashed to his left and right. Consequently, Ānanda’s eyes were bewildered and his head shook.
The Buddha asked him, “Is it my hand that moves, or is it your vision that moves? He replied, “The Buddha’s hand does not remain still;
yet even my nature of seeing has no stillness—how could there be anything that is ‘not remaining’? The Buddha asked again, “Why was your head shaking today? He replied:
As the light moved from left to right, his head moved accordingly. The Buddha asked, "Is it your head that moves, or is it your vision that moves?
He replied, "It is my head that moves; as for my nature of seeing, it has no stillness—so who is there to shake?
The Buddha confirmed this, saying, "So it is, so it is," thereby verifying the immovability of the nature of seeing.
This seals the observation that the river does not change;
third, it distinguishes that the nature of seeing is without transition. "Seal" (*yin*) has the meaning of establishing with certainty.

"Observing the river" refers to King Prasenajit seeing the waters of the Ganges when he was three years old, and then seeing the waters of the Ganges again at the age of sixty-two, [finding them] exactly as they were.
There is no difference. To realize this is to know that from youth to old age, although the physical form undergoes transformation, the seeing itself does not transform.
That which changes is subject to extinction; that which is unchanging fundamentally has neither birth nor death. This demonstrates that the nature of seeing is without transition.
This is compared to the way one’s hanging hand leaves nothing behind;
it is the fourth point, distinguishing that the nature of seeing is without decrease. "Compared to" (*bi*) means "just as" or "by way of analogy. Regarding "the hanging hand":

in the sutra, the World-Honored One was in the midst of the great assembly and pointed downward with his wheel-marked hand, asking, "Is this upright or is it inverted? Ānanda replied: [that which is upright is the Buddha’s body, and that which is inverted is the bodies of sentient beings].
The people of the world consider this to be inverted. The Buddha asked, "What do you take to be upright? They replied, "Pointing upward is upright.

The Buddha said, "Originally it was one hand; what is inverted and what is upright? It is nothing more than the hand and the tail having been exchanged. To illustrate this by analogy regarding the seeing of nature (*jìng-xìng*):
if one awakens, there is no increase; if one is deluded, there is no decrease. It is exactly like the downward-pointing finger: though it is inverted, the hand itself remains unchanged.
Lost. Although the upper part [the head] may be upright, the hand likewise has no attainment.
This distinguishes the "eight returns";
the fifth distinguishes that the seeing-nature has no place to return. "Distinguish" (biàn) means to point out clearly; "return" (huán) means to go back. It is like borrowing...
The things of others originally do not belong to oneself; in the end, they must surely return to their original owner. Regarding the "eight returns," the Sūtra says:
"Luminosity returns to the solar orb," and so on, until the eighth: "clarity returns to a cloudless sky. As for this seeing-nature of yours that perceives these eight kinds, to whom should it return?
Therefore, you should know that all things which can return are not your own property; they cannot [be yours].
As for that which "returns," to what thing does it belong? This demonstrates that the nature of seeing has no point of return; it is precisely the true nature of the person.
When distinguished from all other things, it neither expands nor contracts.

The sixth [point] reveals that the nature of seeing is all-pervasive. "Selecting" (*zhe*) means to discern various objects—namely, everything from the celestial palaces above down to the great earth below;
whatever various things one raises one's eyes to observe must necessarily possess the nature of seeing, regardless of what you select.
"Extending" (*shu*) means to expand; "contracting" (*shu*) means to withdraw. Regarding the "neither-nor": it is like seeing the sky upon leaving one's door, yet the nature of seeing...
It pervades all of space; it is not that you have expanded it to make it great. When you enter a room and perceive its nature, it stops at the size of that single chamber;
it is not that you have contracted it to make it small. Whether great or small, these belong entirely to external objects.
That which perceives is omnipresent—could it be anyone other than you?
There is neither right nor wrong. This causes one to realize that the true mind is pure and perfect; it is only through delusion that it appears as form and emptiness, or as hearing and seeing.

This seventh section reveals that the nature of vision is exclusively true. "There is no 'is'" refers to the fact that all things are merely objects; there is no such thing as a "seeing" that exists independently.
"Nothing that is not [seeing]" means that when minutely illuminated, there is nothing that is not seeing. This precisely examines and shatters the two paths of right and wrong.
"Causing one to awaken" below refers to comprehending the single principle of true nature, thereby transcending the two paths of right and wrong. "Causing."

"Let" means to cause [one] to awaken. "Awaken" means to comprehend and understand. This mind is fundamentally not any of the dharmas; thus it is called "pure. It is fully endowed with all dharmas; thus it is called "perfect.
It is purely one and without delusion; thus it is called "true. As for "form and emptiness," this is merely citing one example from among the six sense objects.
"Those who have heard and seen" refers to two of the six sense faculties mentioned briefly here. The meaning is this:

regarding all phenomena of the sense organs and their objects discussed above, one can neither say they exist nor say they do not exist; what, then, is this thing? Ultimately, who is it that can speak of it?
As one continues to doubt in this manner, suddenly the mass of doubt is shattered, and the True Eye [is revealed].
It appears that not a single dharma exists. As the ancient masters said, "The entire earth is this very self. Only then can one believe they do not deceive us.
From this point on, one realizes that the unchanging essence of one's own mind possesses the function of responding to conditions;

thus it is said: "Once the pure, perfect, and true mind is awakened, the illusory dust-objects of form and emptiness, as well as the sense-faculties of hearing and seeing, [are seen for what they are]."
It is merely nature. It is false, illusory, and not real. The pure, perfect true mind is the unchanging essence;
form, emptiness, hearing, and seeing are its functions that accord with conditions. Since both essence and function are real, it is said to be "only real."

Having already realized that [the self] is delusory, one still harbors doubts regarding its confusion and intermingling; therefore, he further refutes the causes of "spontaneity" (svabhāva) and "conditionality" (pratītyasamutpāda).

The eighth [section] reveals that the nature of seeing is neither conditional nor spontaneous. The word "ji" (already) indicates that the matter has been addressed but not yet concluded; "shang" (still) indicates...

"Still" (*yòu*) means to be muddled and confused; it conveys the sense that a matter has not yet been thoroughly penetrated. "Natural causality" (*zìrán yīnyuán*) refers to the conceptual reckonings regarding the nature of ordinary people and non-Buddhists.

Because non-Buddhists do not realize that the self-nature follows conditions, they falsely reckon upon the *pradhāna* (the primal principle) or the *puruṣa* (the divine self) as being able to produce all things.
Alternatively, they reckon upon Maheśvara as the producer, asserting that things arise and perish naturally without depending on causes and conditions.

Furthermore, because ordinary beings do not realize that the essence of the mind is unchanging, they may reckon that all phenomena arise from themselves as the cause, or arise from others as the condition, or arise through the combination of self and other as both cause and condition. Their intention is this:

although there has been neither right nor wrong above, and although they have awakened to the fact that the numinous mind is beyond dependence, yet it remains unchanging while following conditions, they still harbor [delusions] regarding the pure, perfect, true mind. This is an illusion.

Regarding the hearing and seeing of the emptiness of form, one still harbors doubts and has not yet attained thorough penetration; therefore, it is said that there is still suspicion of confusion and intermingling.
This is precisely because the true light has not yet been fully transcended. Consequently, various conceptual constructions arise in vain:
some reckon that self and other arise together as causes and conditions, which the Buddha refutes by means of the unchanging essence of the mind; others reckon that there is no cause.
Consequently, this naturally leads to confusion with the non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika). Therefore, the Buddha employs his wondrous function of responding to conditions to refute them;

since both [the views of the non-Buddhists and those who cling to the literal] are based on deluded sentiments, they must be refuted. Indeed, this principle of the unchanging responding to conditions while responding to conditions without changing is the fundamental tenet of the Tathāgata’s teaching and the essential discourse for entering into the Truth.
This demonstrates that "seeing seeing" is not seeing.

The ninth [section] reveals the wondrous nature of true essence—the clarity and luminosity of awakening—which not only transcends the deluded sentiments of ordinary people and externalists, but can also distance one from the dharma-views of the provisional and the Lesser Vehicle.
Therefore, it is demonstrated through the principle that "seeing seeing" is not seeing. "Demonstrates" (shi) means to point out and reveal.
The first instance of the character "jian" (see) refers to the nature of pure truth; it is the wondrously enlightened and luminous nature. It is like the pure moon.
The second instance of the character "jian" refers to the essence of mixed delusion; it is the essence of the eye-faculty’s reflected function.
As shown in the eight successive sections above, all instances of "seeing" take the seeing-portion of the seeing-essence and [conjoin it] with the objective realm.

By contrasting the *xiàng-fen* (objective aspect) with the *yì* (meaning/intention), it is intended to clarify that the *jiàn-fen* (perceiving aspect) is not the *xiàng-fen*; this can be clearly understood. Yet, this has not yet fully exposed the ultimate point.

Now, suddenly bringing forth the first character "view" (*jiàn*), one refers to the essence of the *zì-zèng-fen* (self-verifying aspect) which verifies the *zì-zèng-zì-zèng-fen* (aspect that verifies the self-verifying aspect);
this is something even the *jiàn-fen* of the "essence of seeing" (*jiàn-jīng*) cannot reach, let alone the *xiàng-fen* of form and emptiness.

Ah! If one awakens to the realization that appearance and nature are devoid of inherent existence, and that the entire body [of reality] is the illusory function of the self-attesting mind responding to conditions,

then the doubt regarding the pure, perfect, and true mind being falsely transformed into form and emptiness and thereby becoming confused and defiled will melt away like ice and crumble like a fortress.

Combining individual karma with the commonality of shared destiny, this points to that which is produced by deluded vision. For now, one person is used as an analogy for many people, and one country for all countries;
in total, it reveals that the vessel-world and the sense-faculties of the body are nothing but a single delusion.
From shallow to deep, and from narrow to broad, although the delusion is manifested through many methods, that which is ultimately revealed is only the True.
The tenth [section] clarifies the remaining subtle doubts by explaining the progression and regression of individual karma (*prātibhinnakarma*) and common destiny (*sabhāgatā*) together.

"Together" (*saṃyukta*) means to manifest through comparison. "Individual karma" refers to karma created by a single person alone; "common destiny" refers to karma created collectively by a multitude.
Although these two—individual and common—are distinct, they are no different in their falsity. This is because, through the false perception of individual karma...
This is easy to understand. For example, suppose a person has a cataract (red film) over one eye; when looking at a lamp-light, they see a circular halo.
This halo exists only for the person with the diseased eye, while those without the disease do not see it. Therefore, it is easy to know that the circular halo is unreal.
Furthermore, consider an inauspicious phenomenon in the heavens seen by the entire nation; who would doubt its unreality? Thus, [the shared experience] is of the same category.
False views are difficult to discern; it is by relying on the beings of that realm—who do not see or hear [the same things]—that one can manifest their falsity.

This requires the comparative manifestation of two perspectives; hence, it is called "conjunction. From "Furthermore" (*qie yi xia*) onwards, the text provides the formal comparison and manifestation.

The intent is to use a single individual whose distinct karma (*bieye*) is easy to understand as an analogy for the many individuals of the same class (*tongfen*) whose karma is difficult to know, thereby making the latter clear.

Having understood this, one makes what is difficult to know easy to understand. Again, using the ease of knowing a single country as an analogy for the difficulty of knowing various countries, one makes the difficult easy to know;
expanding and extending this further, one uses the multiplicity of various countries as an analogy for the pervasiveness of the ten directions.
This collectively reveals all that exists: internally, the root-bodies of sentient beings, and externally, the vessel-worlds of the lands.

The defiled lands of outflows are likewise but delusions within Bodhi. If one discusses this from the perspective of ultimate truth, regarding the three lands—both the environment and its inhabitants—and the nine realms as a single vision, all are identical to circular reflections.

Only the pure Dharma-body of the Buddha-realm, the true realm of tranquil light, may be called that which is not a circular reflection. From the shallow downward, the preceding eight [realms] are concluded and revealed.
The first instance is shallow, while the ninth instance is deep; thus it is said, "from shallow to deep.
One person is narrow, while one nation is broad; one nation is narrow, while many nations are broad; thus it is said, "from narrow to broad.
The meaning is that although the foregoing has employed various methods—shallow and deep, broad and narrow—to manifest its [the Dharma's] essence.
Delusion. Who would know that delusion has no self-nature, and that its entire substance is itself the True? Therefore it is said: "That which is manifested is only the True.
Second, the extensive enumeration of the four categories and seven elements, demonstrating that the entirety of delusion is itself the True. Part two: first, the headings and enumeration;
second, the actual demonstration. Now, the first.

Therefore, the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are further cited, extensively including the seven great elements, all of which are harmonized and integrated into the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

This section provides a broad enumeration of the major headings to demonstrate that all delusion is itself reality. Thus, the phrase "therefore" (*gu*) serves as a transition from the preceding to the following;
"furthermore" (*you*) carries the sense of elevating the subject. That is to say, the five aggregates, six bases, twelve entrances, and eighteen elements constitute the four [categories].

The "Sections" (*ko*) are passages in the Sūtra that reveal principle through phenomena. The "Great Elements"—earth, water, fire, wind, space, the sense faculties, and consciousness—are the "Seven Greats.
These are passages in the Sūtra that discuss nature through its manifestations. Now, principle and phenomenon, as well as nature and manifestation, are fundamentally not distinct dharmas.
